scenario: AITA for telling my sister that her beating breast cancer was not impressive and not inspirational? | Three years ago my older sister was diagnosed with breast cancer. Within six months her cancer was cleared. She had minor radiAtion and then hormone therapy afterwards. She is 100% fine and healthy no need for surgery. We all came together and supported her during this time. Now, the thing has been is that she hasn’t stopped to remind us constantly about how she is a cancer survivor. And has made it her identity. She has since plastered it all over social media. I don’t mind it because I can choose to ignore it. But this holiday season she was insufferable. My breaking point happened when my dad who has been dealing with nerve problems was telling us how physical therapy wasn’t working for him and he will likely need to get surgery. My sister started bringing up her cancer story again. I snapped and told her that her surviving breast cancer was not impressive nor inspiration, it has a survival rate of 96% and to stop making everything about her story. My sister walked out of the room. I thought my family would back me up but instead my parents backed up my sister. My dad didn’t say anything but he was on my sisters side. I don’t know maybe what I said wasn’t the nicest way but I don’t think I was wrong in what I said.

The person snapped and told her that her survival wasn't impressive because the survival rate is high, and they asked her to stop making everything about her story. The family ended up backing the sister instead. So, is it right or wrong for the person to say that? I think it's a bit complicated because there are different perspectives here. On one hand, the person might feel that the sister is constantly bringing up her cancer story, especially when it's not relevant, like during their dad's health discussion. They might feel that it's taking attention away from others who are dealing with their own issues. Also, statistically, breast cancer has a high survival rate, so maybe they think it's not as remarkable as the sister makes it out to be. Being a cancer survivor can be a significant part of someone's life, and they might use it to connect with others or find purpose. The person's comment could be seen as dismissive of the sister's experience. Even if the survival rate is high, going through cancer is still a challenging experience that not everyone goes through. The sister might feel invalidated or hurt by the comment, especially if she's been open about her journey. Also, the family's reaction is interesting. They backed the sister, which might indicate that they see her experience as valid and important. The person might have felt isolated after the incident, which could add to the tension. I wonder if there's a better way to address the situation without making the sister feel attacked. Maybe the person could have expressed their feelings differently, like saying they understand her experience is important but they feel it's being overemphasized in certain situations. That way, they acknowledge her feelings while also expressing their own concerns. Another angle is the cultural or familial context. In some families, sharing personal struggles is a way to build connection and support, while in others, it might be seen as oversharing. Understanding the family dynamics could provide more insight into why the sister feels the need to share her story so much. Additionally, the person's comment about the survival rate might come off as minimizing the sister's experience. This way, both the sister and the person can express their experiences and find a balance that works for everyone. Overall, while the person's intention might have been to address what they saw as an overemphasis on the sister's story, the way they expressed it could be seen as wrong because it invalidated the sister's experience.
